title: Speed up ethernet entry (manuf and wka) parsing.
description:
This saves around 3% time (profiling a small capture file) at startup.
parse_ether_address_fast() was returning FALSE in some cases
where it shouldn't have, i.e.
- the test for the having hex chars incorrectly discarded any case where the
  msb of any address octet is set, i.e. any value from 80 to f0.
- it now allows ':' and '-' as a separator (so that many of the wka entries
  also match).

notes.body: assigned to @Lekensteyn

@Lekensteyn - can you please check this?  Did I completely miss the point with the (num1 | num2 | num3) & 0x80  test?

I wasn't sure about making the fast version accept '-' as a separator.  But if we didn't, it it would currently try and fail for every address in 'wka'.  Where it does test for both separators, for the dominant ':' (manuf) case, it should lazily not be checking for the '-' case.

The `(num0 | num1 | num2) & 0x80` test is supposed to catch catch the `-1` value which as unsigned number would be `0xff`. Then for `(x << 4) | y`, if either `x` or `y` are 0xff, then the whole result would have the MSB bit set.

So the new "not a hexadecimal number" check is just a more verbose way to check for the same thing. If this is not needed for the speed improvement, I suggest reverting it.

If we have a an entry such as this one from manuf:

00:00:80        CrayComm

num2 will be 0x80,  so the entry is rejected by parse_ether_address_fast() and needs to be parsed using parse_ether_address() instead.

I have a working version that stores the ASCII hex chars in a gint16 array. Then, -1 (0xffff) extends beyond the bits that may legitimately be set, and the test for non-hex characters becomes (num0 | num1 | num2) & 0xff00).  I will compare the speed of this against the current patch - I may be missing something but it looks to me as if the current code in wrongly misses lots of chances to use this faster path, and I thought the speedup work worthwhile (something like 14 ms every time wireshark or tshark starts).
I made this change.

>making the fast version accept '-' as a separator

What is the point of two separators? The standard uses only -, but we use only :. 
How are you parsing MA-M and MA-S BTW, that are not 3 bytes, but more and first part (3 bytes of that bigger part) belong to IEEE Registration Authority? See https://regauth.standards.ieee.org/standards-ra-web/pub/view.html#registries

I don't know this code well at all.

If you look at tools/make-manuf.py, the various .csv files it fetches from standards-oui.ieee.org all have the same format in the 2nd column, i.e. the hex pattern appears with no separators at all, but rather the ':' separator is added by (I think) prefix_to_oui(). Notice that the 36-bit entries appear as 5 bytes in the file - these are padded out to 6 and given the '/36' suffix.

wka (which uses '-' as a separator), is curated by hand.

I don't know why ':' was chosen for manuf.  I don't think it would make a measurable difference to parsing speed if they both used the same separator though.  The parsing code would become a little easier to understand.  I refrained from teaching the _fast function about other mask lengths that appear in wka.

@geraldcombs - do you know if there was a good reason for them to differ in separator characters?

> @geraldcombs - do you know if there was a good reason for them to differ in separator characters?

I don't recall off the top of my head. As mentioned above, [the IEEE uses either no separators or hyphens (dashes) between each octet](https://standards.ieee.org/content/dam/ieee-standards/standards/web/documents/tutorials/eui.pdf), but colons are in common use elsewhere such as the `ifconfig` command on most Unix/Linux systems, `ip` on Linux, and `wmic` on Windows. As I recall, some systems (Cisco catOS?) used dots, e.g. 0000.1111.2222.
I don't plan on changing the separator in wka for this change.

You can look into https://www.wireshark.org/tools/oui-lookup.html try to paste in 74-1A-E0, you will get this (from MA-M /28), as you can see 74:1A:E0 itself belong to IEEE RA, then you add 4 bits and then the last 20 bits are given to some company.

```
74:1A:E0 IEEE Registration Authority
74:1A:E0:00:00:00/28 Huano International Technology Limited
74:1A:E0:10:00:00/28 Socionext Inc.
74:1A:E0:20:00:00/28 Nura Holdings Pty Ltd
74:1A:E0:30:00:00/28 Philips Personal Health Solutions
74:1A:E0:40:00:00/28 Revl Inc.
74:1A:E0:50:00:00/28 Fujian Taili Communication Technology Co.,Ltd
74:1A:E0:60:00:00/28 Blocks Wearables Inc.
74:1A:E0:70:00:00/28 BÄR Bahnsicherung AG
74:1A:E0:80:00:00/28 Broadcast Wireless Systems Ltd
74:1A:E0:90:00:00/28 Private
74:1A:E0:A0:00:00/28 Saiercom Corporation
74:1A:E0:B0:00:00/28 Shen Zhen Yingjiachuang Electronics Technology Co.,Ltd.
74:1A:E0:C0:00:00/28 bistos.co.ltd
74:1A:E0:D0:00:00/28 Voltaware Services Limited
74:1A:E0:E0:00:00/28 ITS Partner (O.B.S) S.L.
```

Now, this is not all. I will not talk about /36 (MA-S), but there is also Company ID blocks. Company ID can be recognised simply by checking the first byte. It should end in 0b1010.
The point here is that CID does have local administered bit set.

Now there is also deprecated IAB. It is like MA-S, but it does not overlap and used only 2 OUI that belong to IEEE RA.

>having hex chars seems to discard any case where the msb
of any address octet is set

What does this mean? You say that something like 00:01:00 will not work? But it does, 00:01:00 belongs to Equip'Trans, the same about 00:00:01, Xerox Corporation! I am confused. And of course 01:00:00 should be dismissed as it is multicast MAC address, because of CID we cannot get rid of 02:00:00.

If you look at the parsing, there is a _fast() parsing function that works with limited formats, and a slower fallback version that is tried if _fast() fails.

My change is to make more of the address strings get handled by the _fast() function.  There was what looked like a cool trick to spot if unrecognised characters appeared instead of hex digits, but it didn't work if the msb of any of of the octets was set.  So with this change, many more addresses get handled without dropping back to the slower parsing function.

The 2nd change was to also accept the '-' separator (used with 'wka') in _fast().  This doesn't mean that all of the entries get handled - there are some entries with different lengths of masks that _fast() doesn't handle (but could be made to).  I thought this was reasonable as it should slow down the fast function only very slightly where the ':' separator is used.

>if the msb of any of of the octets was set

Are you talking about multicast bit in the first octet?

Check the change - maybe you will see something I missed.  The test was something like (0x80 & (num1 | num2 | num3)).

The test was used for the 1st 3 bytes, and if there were 6, on the last 3.
Good idea.  Will try to do some more testing later on and update patch.
Done.
